1236-first-across-the-continent-the-stor:
Noah Brooks tells the story of Lewis and Clark's expedition, the first American party to cross the continent to the Pacific and back. The narrative follows the Corps of Discovery up the Missouri, over the Rockies, and down the Columbia, with Sacagawea, bears, and winter camps along the way.

Brooks writes for young readers, with maps of the route and a plain, stirring style. The book gives the expedition's whole arc in one volume. It suits readers who want the great American exploration tale told straight and well. Brooks tells the great expedition straight, and the tale still stirs.
12510-targum-or-metrical-translations-fr:
George Borrow's Targum offers metrical translations from thirty languages and dialects, gathered over years of philological work. Borrow admits, with diffidence, that he often failed to give his versions the cast and turn that make much of an original's beauty. Rendering diction into tolerable verse, he says, is easy beside catching tone.

The pieces range widely, from a Persian poem about a raven and a nightingale's nest to songs of many peoples. Borrow presents them as selections from a huge, undigested mass, not a polished system. The book shows a nineteenth-century linguist at work, curious, restless and fond of strange tongues.
13571-notes-and-queries-index-of-volume-:
An index to the second volume of Notes and Queries, May to December 1850, gathers in alphabetical order the whole half-year of antiquarian talk. Entries run from solemnization of matrimony and admiration to Adur, Aeneas Silvius, aerostation, and the Darby Ram, each with page numbers for the original notes and queries.

Later letters cover Dodd's Church History, dragons and their origin, the authorship of disputed tracts, and Scott's Waverley. While L entries take in Long Friday, Lonkin, the Lord Mayor's Show, lost tribes, and Love's Labour Lost. The index turns a scattered weekly into a usable reference book, letting a reader find a small fact months after it first appeared.
13762-report-of-mr-w-e-cormack-s-journey:
W. E. Cormack reported this journey in search of the Beothuk, called Red Indians, of Newfoundland. He read the report before the Boeothick Institution at St. John's on January 12, 1828. The institution aimed to open contact with the Beothuk and record their language, customs, and history. Cormack travelled inland with Native guides through forest and river country.

He found old camps and signs of a people long undisturbed, then abandoned. An old mountaineer guide was moved by the empty rendezvous. Cormack's account is short but first-hand and sober. It documents a people already vanishing under colonial pressure. The report remains a key source for Beothuk history and for Newfoundland exploration.
13882-john-thorndyke-s-cases-related-by-:
R. Austin Freeman gathered Dr. John Thorndyke's cases in this volume, related by Christopher Jervis, M.D. Thorndyke, a medical detective, solves crimes by science: footprints, dust, and documents. Cases include the man with nailed shoes, the stranger's latchkey, and the blue sequin. The Moabite cipher, the mandarin's pearl, and the aluminium dagger follow.

Freeman dedicates the book to a friend, recalling evenings spent with microscope and camera. Thorndyke reasons aloud as he walks a shore left by the retiring tide. Each story teaches forensic method through plot. The collection helped found the scientific detective story. Fans of Holmes will enjoy Thorndyke's cooler, more technical style.
14032-an-enquiry-into-the-truth-of-the-t:
John Williams, writing as a Welsh scholar, tests the old tale that Prince Madog ab Owen Gwynedd reached America about 1170, three centuries before Columbus. Place names supply his first clues: Curaçao, Cape Breton, and other coastal words may hide Welsh roots. Montezuma's remark to Cortés, that Mexican chiefs came from foreign stock, adds a second thread. Old manuscripts, heralds' copies, and bards' records fill the rest.

Caution marks the method. Williams weighs each source, notes where copyists corrected each other, and admits where conjecture outruns proof. Dr. Powel's work on Guttun Owen's compilations receives close attention, since a herald's office would hold the papers in question. Modern readers will judge the Welsh voyage unproven, but the enquiry remains a learned example of early historical criticism, built from language, chronicle, and careful doubt.
14346-an-historical-relation-of-the-isla:
Robert Knox wrote this 1681 account after near twenty years captive in Ceylon. He had sailed with Englishmen who were held on the island, and at last made an escape. The East India Company praised him as a man of truth and urged him to print his tale. Knox tells of kings, courts, towns, and life in the island's hills and coasts. His prose keeps the spelling and voice of his own age.

Knox shows a king who seizes nobles, and men glad to act as his executioners for place and office. When a man fell, his sons and brothers might be cut off or jailed, lest they plot revenge. The captives ate rice with flesh, fish, or eggs, and read Rogers' Practice of Piety in the cool of evening. Fever towns, sick years, and hunger marked their lot. The book stands as a plain record of a captivity.
1448-heidi:
Johanna Spyri tells of Heidi, a small Swiss orphan sent to live with her stern grandfather, the Alm-Uncle, high in the Alps. Goats, mountains, and fresh air heal both the child and the old man. Spyri wrote Heidi in 1881, and it soon travelled the world in translation.

Heidi's later stay in Frankfurt, with Clara and her household, tests her love of home, before she returns to the mountains. Spyri's story, loved worldwide, celebrates nature, kindness, and the bonds of family. The Alps, with goats and mountain air, give the story its health and its joy.
1971-erewhon-revisited-twenty-years-late:
Samuel Butler's Erewhon Revisited, signed at the close on May 1, 1901, returns to the country he invented in Erewhon in 1872, twenty years after Mr. Higgs escaped in a balloon with Arowhena. Butler asks what course events would take after that apparently miraculous ascent, given a people in the conditions supposed to exist in Erewhon.

The sequel follows Higgs's son, who travels to the country his father discovered, and finds a religion built around the balloon ascent itself. Butler writes the satire with the same cool wit as the original. The book's joke is double: a new faith founded on a misunderstanding, and a father meeting the son of his own legend.
25878-commentary-upon-the-maya-tzental-p:
William E. Gates, of Point Loma, California, gives a close study of the Maya-Tzental Perez Codex for the Peabody Museum at Harvard, printed in November 1910. The codex, a screenfold book of Maya glyphs, gets a full commentary, a printed text in type, and a fresh index of its signs. Gates worked out the glyph classes as one task, so the codex study also served his wider work on Maya writing.

A closing note takes up the linguistic problem of the Maya glyphs, asking how the signs map to speech and sense. Gates weighs color facts, checks his readings against the larger Dresden Codex, and notes that the Perez book, being smaller, could be finished sooner. The paper stands as a careful step toward reading a script long locked to scholars.
2627-on-the-method-of-zadig-essay-1-from:
Thomas Henry Huxley opens his Science and Hebrew Tradition essays with the method of Zadig, named for Voltaire's hero who reads a trail from faint marks. Huxley takes Cuvier's praise of Zadig's surer mark as his motto, and argues that science often works backward from clues to causes.

The essay defends retrospective prophecy, the power to infer past events from present traces, as a true function of science. Huxley writes with combative clarity, turning a literary allusion into a method. Readers get a short, sharp lesson in how naturalists reason, and why such reasoning deserves trust.
26770-notes-and-queries-index-of-volume-:
This volume indexes Notes and Queries, volume three, January to June 1851, the medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, is When found, make a note of. The index is alphabetical by contributor and subject, with page numbers pointing back to notes, queries, and replies.

Early entries cover A on Tanthony, the song Winifreda, Dutch folk lore, the Martin family, swords used in dress, and Moore's Almanack. Further A entries treat abbots in the English church, Abel represented with horns, the two Dr. Abercrombys, the ace of diamonds, mistletoe on oaks, and the phrase under the rose. F entries run from Cranmer's descendants and the Prince of Wales's feathers to Nicholas Ferrar's Digest and Concordance, the names of the ferret, and the derivation of fest.
2923-the-method-by-which-the-causes-of-t:
Thomas Henry Huxley's third lecture to working men asks by what method the causes of organic nature can be discovered. Having sketched past and present phenomena in two earlier talks, Huxley now turns to the great problem itself, what knowledge we have of the causes behind the facts. The lecture treats the origin of living beings as a question for evidence, not assertion.

Huxley compares scientific reasoning to detecting a burglar, the method Newton and Laplace used for the heavens, applied here with extra care. A single crack or flaw in a hypothesis, he warns, can undo it. The lecture gives readers the logic of Darwin's case in plain terms, and it still reads as a fine lesson in how science argues.
29867-notes-and-queries-index-of-volume-:
This volume is the index to the fifth volume of Notes and Queries, covering January to June 1852. The journal billed itself as a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, genealogists, and others. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, reads When found, make a note of it. The index gathers half a year of questions, answers, and notes into one alphabetical run.

Entries under A alone show the range: Welsh names, the Abbot's letters to the clergy, and the Aberdeen Banking Company. Scottish regalia, Addison and his hymns, and the meaning of Chatterbox sit beside Junius, sword swallowing, and the number of the children of Israel. For a reader hunting a small fact of 1852, this index is the key to a crowded, curious journal.
30311-modus-vivendi:
Walter Bupp tells Modus Vivendi in Analog, September 1961, with pictures by Schoenherr. It is difficult to live with someone who is Different, the tagline says, since he must, because he is Different, live by other ways. What makes it so difficult is that, for some reason, he thinks you are Different. By the time the narrator reaches the office, he is jittery as a bride, the day having started wrong.

He woke washed out, at the weights, which felt as heavy as the Pyramids. A telepath trailed him all the way from the subway to the offices he shares with Mike Renner. Ready for a scrap, he finds Mike seated and staring at a caller across the table in their law library. Without a book or sheet of foolscap on the walnut, work not started, both lie in wait for him. The Grievance Committee, Mike says in fury.
31714-the-art-of-needle-work-from-the-ea:
Edited by the Countess of Wilton, this third edition was published in London in 1841. It traces the art of needlework from the earliest ages and includes notices of ancient historical tapestries. Dedicated to the Queen Dowager, it presents needlework as an art ennobled by royal practice and example.

Its preface argues that the needle serves everyone, from palace to cottage and from cradle to grave, yet has lacked its due record while the sword has been praised without limit. Readers get a Victorian history of embroidery and tapestry, written to give a woman's art its place in historical and social record.
5173-the-religion-of-the-samurai-a-study:
Kaiten Nukariya's Religion of the Samurai, published in 1913, presents Zen philosophy and discipline as practised in China and Japan. Chapters trace Zen's history in both countries, then explain its view of the universe as scripture, of Buddha as universal spirit, of human nature, and of training the mind through meditation.

Nukariya, a professor at Keio University and a Soto Buddhist college in Tokyo, wrote for Western readers curious about the faith of the samurai class. The book remains a clear early English introduction to Zen thought, joining history, doctrine, and practice in a single, readable survey.
6036-the-kasi-dah-of-ha-ji-abdu-el-yezdi:
The Kasîdah of Hâjî Abdû El-Yezdî comes translated and annotated by the author's friend and pupil, F. B., who calls it a lay of the higher law. The translator presents it as a work in advance of its time, not fearing collision with the forms of higher culture.

Its principles hold happiness and misery equally divided in the world. They make self-cultivation with due regard to others the sole object of life, and prize affection, sympathy, and pity as man's highest enjoyments. Judgment, it urges, should be suspended, with suspicion of facts as idlest superstitions. Destructive in look, the poem is essentially reconstructive.
an-enquiry-into-the-truth-of-the-traditi: John Williams enquires into the truth of the tradition that Prince Madog ab Owen Gwynedd discovered America about the year 1170. Published in London, with a list of errata left uncorrected, the work weighs Welsh claims against the evidence. It remains a curious chapter in the history of pre-Columbian claims.
an-historical-relation-of-the-island-cey: Robert Knox gives an historical relation of the island of Ceylon in the East Indies, with an account of his long captivity there with other Englishmen and his miraculous escape. Published in London, the book describes Kandyan life, customs, and rule from inside. Knox's captivity narrative became a classic source on seventeenth-century Sri Lanka.
britannica-1911-ben-ledi:
Ben Ledi, Gaelic for “the hill of God,” is a mountain of Perthshire, Scotland, 2,875 feet high, five miles by road north-west of Callander. It stands close to some of the most romantic scenery in the Highlands. Scott’s poem The Lady of the Lake made its name widely known.

The name is thought to point back to Beltane rites once held on the summit. A cairn raised there in 1887 marked Queen Victoria’s jubilee. On one flank lies a small tarn called Lochan nan Corp, “the little loch of the dead.” The name comes from an accident to a funeral party in which, the entry says, two hundred lives were lost.
britannica-1911-capistrano-giovanni-di:
Giovanni di Capistrano (1386–1456) was an Italian friar and inquisitor. This 1911 Britannica entry tells his hard, restless life. He was born in the village of Capistrano, in the Abruzzi. His family had come to Italy with the Angevins. He first lived a wholly secular life. He married and became a successful magistrate. War and politics then ruined him in captivity. He lost his young wife in the same fall.

In despair Capistrano entered the Franciscan order. He gave himself to the strictest ascetic life. The popes sent him on mission after mission. As legate and inquisitor he struck many groups. He persecuted Fraticelli and others in several lands. Above all he hunted the Hussites of Bohemia. He blocked any talks between Rome and the Bohemians. After Constantinople fell, he raised troops for a crusade. His force helped lift the siege of Belgrade in 1455. He died that October, and was canonized in 1690.
britannica-1911-carnot-marie-francois-sa:
Marie François Sadi Carnot (1837–1894) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on the fourth president of the third French Republic. Born at Limoges, he trained as a civil engineer at the École Polytechnique and the École des Ponts et Chaussées. In 1870 the government of national defence charged him with organising resistance in three departments. He entered the National Assembly in 1871 and later held the public works and finance ministries.

When scandal forced President Grévy out in December 1887, Carnot's clean record won him the presidency, with 616 votes out of 827. He took office as General Boulanger openly threatened the republic, and he answered with well-judged public appearances. His term covered the centenary of 1789 and the Paris Exhibition of that year, both read as public votes for the republic. The entry follows his steady hand through short-lived ministries and socialist unrest.
britannica-1911-credi-lorenzo-di:
Lorenzo di Credi (1459–1537), an Italian artist whose surname was Barducci, was born at Florence. He began as a journeyman with Andrea del Verrocchio, alongside Leonardo da Vinci and Perugino. The entry calls him the least gifted of that group. His faces show a calm, smiling beatitude, and his pigments have the polish of enamel. Yet his work lacks the life Leonardo gave his figures and the ease Perugino could show.

Credi held a solid local practice at Florence and was often asked for expert judgment. He advised on the cathedral front in 1491, its lantern in 1498, and the placing of Michelangelo's David in 1504. He painted no frescoes and few large church pictures, spending most time on easel pieces worked with minute care. Many Madonnas by him survive in European galleries. His best altar-piece, a Virgin and Child with saints, stands in Pistoia cathedral.
britannica-1911-gaddi:
Gaddi was the name of four Florentine painters, a father, his son and two grandsons. Gaddo Gaddi, friend of Cimabue and of Giotto, was a painter and mosaicist who may have been born about 1260 and died about 1333. He is credited with the mosaics in the portico of Santa Maria Maggiore in Rome, dated about 1308, and he laid the base of a large family fortune. No panel picture by him is known to survive.

His son Taddeo (about 1300–1366) worked with Giotto, ranked among his followers, and traded as a merchant. His frescoes fill the Baroncelli chapel in Santa Croce, and as an architect he supplied the plans for the Ponte Vecchio in 1336 and carried on Giotto's campanile. Taddeo's son Agnolo, who died in 1396, painted the legend of the Cross in eight frescoes in Santa Croce, but gave his middle age to trade in Venice. The fourth, Giovanni, died in 1383.
britannica-1911-lodi:
Lodi is a town and bishop's seat in Piedmont, Italy. Milan lies twenty and a half miles north-west by rail. A low hill above the Adda's right bank holds it, 230 feet over the sea. Town count in 1901 was 19,970. The commune held 26,827. Rich dairy land rings the town on all sides.

The cathedral dates to 1158, with a Gothic front. The Incoronata church of 1488 is an eight-sided dome of great grace. Frescoes by the Piazza family fill it. San Francesco, of the 1200s, holds paintings of the 1300s. Cheese leads trade: Lodi makes more Parmesan than Parma. Linen, silk, majolica, and chemicals add their share. Old Laus Pompeia lay three and a half miles west. Its site is now Lodi Vecchio, with the old church of St Bassiano. Roads to Milan, Placentia, and Cremona split there in Roman days.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-achille-gagli:
Achille Gagliardi was a Paduan ascetic writer and spiritual director, born in 1537, who died at Modena on 6 July 1607. His brilliant Padua University career preceded his 1559 entry into the Society of Jesus with two younger brothers. He taught philosophy at the Roman College and theology at Padua and Milan, and ran several northern Italian houses of his order with success.

He preached, gave retreats, and directed congregations with tireless zeal, and St. Charles Borromeo, Archbishop of Milan, held him in great esteem as theologian and guide. Borromeo took him on pastoral visitations and asked him to publish his popular handbook, Catechismo della fede cattolica, in 1584. His Breve compendio on Christian perfection, printed after his death, was translated into five languages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agnolo-giovan:
Agnolo, Giovanni, and Taddeo Gaddi were Florentine artists. Taddeo was father of Agnolo and Giovanni. Their birth dates are very uncertain: Taddeo probably about 1300, his sons after 1333. Giovanni died in 1383, Agnolo in 1396, the father in 1366. All three lie buried in Florence's Santa Croce. Taddeo was Giotto's godson, spent twenty-four years with him, becoming the most eminent of his many scholars.

Vasari says Taddeo surpassed his master in colour and sometimes in expression. Two signed paintings survive: one in Berlin dated 1333, one at Mogognano dated 1355. His best extant frescoes are in Santa Croce's Giugni Chapel. He is perhaps best known as architect of Florence's Ponte Vecchio and the finer Ponte Trinita downstream, destroyed in the sixteenth century. His son Agnolo's best work is at Prato cathedral and Santa Croce, and he taught Cennino Cennini, whose treatise is the chief source on early Florentine technique.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alberto-arnol: Alberto Arnoldi, also called di Arnoldo, was an Italian sculptor and architect of fourteenth-century Florence. He worked on a colossal group of the Virgin and Child with two angels for the church of Santa Maria del Bigallo from 1359 to 1364. The group was wrongly credited by Vasari to Andrea Pisano. As an architect, Arnoldi directed the works of Florence cathedral about 1358.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrea-gallan:
Andrea Gallandi, an Oratorian scholar, was born at Venice on 7 December 1709 and died there on 12 January 1779, or 1780. He came of an ancient French family. He studied theology and history under Danello Concina, a moralist, and Bernardo de Rossi, a noted scholar. Both stayed friends after he joined the Oratory of Saint Philip Neri.

His reputation rests on the still valuable Bibliotheca veterum patrum antiquorumque scriptorum ecclesiasticorum Graeco-Latina. It was published at Venice from 1765 to 1781 in fourteen volumes, with a second edition. Dedicated to the Venetian Senate, it was unfinished at his death. It gathers 380 ecclesiastical writers of the first seven centuries. Its merit lies in collecting smaller, lesser-known writings rather than works already in print, with Greek originals, Latin translations, and copious notes. He also published treatises by canonists on the origin of canon law in 1778. At his death he left an unpublished thesaurus of ecclesiastical antiquity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-annibale-d-an:
Annibale d'Annibaldi, theologian, born of a Roman senatorial family, died at Rome in 1271. He joined the Dominicans young and studied at Paris. Here he befriended Aquinas and succeeded him at Paris. After teaching in Paris, he was called to Rome in 1246. He served under Alexander IV and Urban IV, made Cardinal in 1262. When Clement IV handed the Two Sicilies to Charles of Anjou in 1265, Annibale headed the commission treating with the monarch.

On a papal mission at Orvieto, the Cardinal died and was buried at San Domenico by his request. He was esteemed for learning and virtues, and Aquinas dedicated Catena Aurea to him. Annibale, besides small treatises now lost, wrote a Sentences commentary and Quodlibeta, ascribed to Thomas and published with his works in 1889. A Paris manuscript calls Annibale a Carmelite turned Cistercian abbot, but Echard shows no such man belonged to either order then.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartholomaeus:
Bartholomaeus Arnoldi, usually called Usingen, was an Augustinian friar and Luther's teacher, born in 1463, who died at Würzburg in 1532. Master in 1491 and doctor of divinity in 1514, he held Erfurt's philosophy and theology chairs for thirty years. With Jodocus Truttfetter he ranked as Erfurt's most illustrious teacher, famed for holiness, intellect, and loyalty to the Church. Lauded as dialectician and logician, he taught Luther in both branches, and Luther held him in affectionate regard.

After the Heidelberg Disputation of May 1518, Luther traveled with him to Erfurt, vainly trying to shake his allegiance. In 1521 he boldly denounced rioters pillaging priests' property, and in 1522 preached cathedral sermons defending the Church. His utterances embittered Luther, who then violently assailed his old teacher. Moved to Würzburg in 1526, he kept fighting the innovators and attended the Diet of Augsburg in 1530.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernardino-ba:
Bernardino Baldi, an Italian poet and scholar, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Urbino in 1553, he died there in 1617 after study at Padua and Rome in mathematics, classics, and Eastern languages. Chaldaic, Arabic, and Persian were among the tongues he learned, a rare range for his age.

Ordained a priest, he became Abbot of Guastalla under Prince Ferrante Gonzaga, holding the post despite long absences until 1609, when Urbino claimed him for his last years. Poems, histories, and learned treatises flowed from a mind the entry treats as a model of Renaissance breadth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carbo-sebasti:
Carlo Sebastiano Berardi was an Italian canonist born at Oneglia in August 1719 who died in 1768. After theology at Savona under the Piarists and ordination, he turned to law at Turin with a focus on canonical jurisprudence. In 1749 he became prefect of Turin's law faculty, and from 1754 until his death he held the chair of canon law there.

His chief work sifted Gratian's Decretum, sorting genuine canons from spurious ones against better manuscripts and explaining hard passages. Critics praised its learning and industry, ranking it behind only Antonio Agostino's work as a critical account of Gratian. They noted slips and occasional over-criticism. Later works covered sacred canons in theory and practice and a church-law textbook the entry warns readers to use with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-casto-innocen:
Casto Innocenzio Ansaldi was an Italian theologian and archaeologist born at Piacenza in March 1710 who died at Turin in 1780. He joined the Dominicans at Parma in 1726. He studied at the Minerva College in Rome from 1733, where he attached himself to Cardinal Orsi. He taught philosophy in Naples at Santa Caterina in 1735. A metaphysics chair followed, then a theology chair created for him by the King of Naples in 1737, held until 1745.

From 1745 to 1770 he taught in turn at Brescia, Ferrara, and Turin, spending twenty years in Turin with great success and repute. Opposed to the scholastic method, he clashed with his order's authorities until Cardinal Quirini and Benedict XIV smoothed matters over. His many volumes, prized for joining theological and historical learning against his day's anti-Christian trends, include a defense of the patriarch Joseph. Another work treats the tradition of natural law's principles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-constantino-b:
Augustus Van Cleef's entry follows Constantino Brumidi, Italian-American painter famed for fresco work in Washington's Capitol, born at Rome in 1805, died at Washington on 19 February 1880. Early fresco talent showed in Roman palaces, including Prince Torlonia's. Under Gregory XVI he worked three years in the Vatican. France's 1849 occupation of Rome decided his emigration; he sailed for America and gained citizenship in 1852.

In New York City he painted portraits, then a Crucifixion fresco in Saint Stephen's Church, with a Martyrdom of Saint Stephen and an Assumption of the Virgin. Returning, he stopped at Washington and offered his services to Quartermaster-General Meigs. Accepted, and commissioned a cavalry captain, he began in the House Agriculture Committee's room at eight dollars a day. His rotunda apotheosis of Washington stayed unfinished at his death, though he decorated much else. Capable if conventional, his bas-relief modelling strikes viewers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cursor-mundi:
A literary entry introduces Cursor Mundi, the Runner of the World, a Middle English poem of nearly 30,000 lines summarizing universal history. Its many surviving manuscripts show it was exceptionally popular. Written in northern England near 1300 by a cleric whose name is unknown, it survives in eight-syllabled couplets, with a new metre for the Passion.

Though it covers all history, the poem gains unity from man's redemption as its theme. A long prologue contrasts vain earthly love in old romances of Arthur, Troy, and Charlemagne with love of Our Lady, who saves from sin and wins heaven's bliss. The poem then tells of the Trinity, the fall of angels, Adam, the patriarchs, and Christ's coming, in a work still central to medieval English studies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-donatello-di-:
Donatello, whose full name was Donato di Nicolo di Betto Bardi, ranks among the great Tuscan sculptors of the Renaissance. Born at Florence about 1386, he was apprenticed young to a goldsmith to learn design. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how at seventeen he went to Rome with his friend Brunelleschi, and the two youths drew and dug for antiquities, chiseling half the week for a living. Brunelleschi chose architecture, while Donatello always put sculpture first.

Still a boy, he carved the wooden crucifix of Santa Croce, and on his return to Florence his work filled churches and squares. The entry, citing Vasari, Lubke, and Perkins, leaves his chronology hard to fix but his rank secure. He died at Florence on 13 December 1466, a founder of Renaissance sculpture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-engaddi:
Engaddi, in Hebrew Fountain of the Kid, was a warm spring and a town on the west shore of the Dead Sea, near its middle. Chronicles identifies it with Asasonthamar, the Amorite city struck by Chodorlahomor in his war on the cities of the plain. Joshua lists it among the cities of Judah in the desert, while Ezekiel shows it as a fishing town.

David hid in the desert of Engaddi, and Saul hunted him even on crags fit only for wild goats. There too Moabites and Ammonites mustered against King Josaphat, and the Song of Songs praises the vineyards of Engaddi. Josephus links it to fine palms and opobalsam. Pliny ranks it second only to Jerusalem for fertility and palms. Today its name lives as Ain Jedi, a small oasis between two wadis, ringed by steep rock.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-gua:
Francesco Guardi, born at Venice in 1712 and dead there in 1793, was a Venetian painter of city views and a pupil of Canaletto, whose style he closely followed. Almost nothing is known of his life beyond a belief that he always lived in Venice and painted scenes of that city and its neighbourhood. He worked with extraordinary speed, finishing a whole picture in three or four days. His paintings, rich and forcible in colour and true in general effect, fall behind Canaletto's in fine detail, solidity, and firm grounding.

They are prized instead for spirited touch and sparkling colour. Examples hang in almost every European gallery, notably Paris, Berlin, Modena, Brussels, Venice, and Verona, while smaller works are in great demand among wealthy collectors. He is credited with nearly a thousand pictures, and Berenson saw him as anticipating Romantic and Impressionist painters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-mar:
Francesco Maria Grimaldi, born at Bologna on 2 April 1618 and dead there on 28 December 1663, was a Jesuit physicist and worthy predecessor of Newton and Huygens. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1632, spent twenty-five years teaching belles-lettres in Jesuit colleges, and gave his later years almost entirely to physics and astronomy. He helped Riccioli test falling bodies between 1640 and 1650, surveyed an arc of the meridian in 1645, and mapped the moon's surface for Riccioli's Almagestum Novum.

Grimaldi gave the moon's mountains and valleys the names of philosophers and astronomers, replacing Hevelius's names drawn from earthly seas and mountains. His chief work was in optics. He first observed diffraction, the spreading of light through a small opening into a cone with a shadow larger than geometry predicts, and first noted the dispersion of sunlight through a prism. His book on light, colour, and the rainbow appeared after his death in 1665.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-red:
Francesco Redi, born at Arezzo on 18 February 1626 and dead at Pisa on 1 March 1698, was an Italian physician, poet, and experimenter. After a medical degree he tutored for the Colonna family at Rome for five years. He then went to Florence in 1654 as physician to Grand Dukes Ferdinand II and Cosimo III. He kept experimenting to improve medicine and surgery while finding time for much literary work. He joined several academies, helped prepare the Crusca dictionary, and taught Tuscan language at Florence in 1666.

His scientific writings include observations on vipers, experiments on the generation of insects, and medical consultations. His poems include the dithyrambs Bacco in Toscana and Arianna Inferma and lyrics both Petrarchian and burlesque in tone. Bacco in Toscana, though marred at times by obscure imagery, stands as the best Italian dithyramb and one of the finest works of the seventeenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-batt:
Giovanni Battista Audiffredi was a Dominican bibliographer and astronomer born at Saorgio near Nice in 1734, who died at Rome in July 1794. He entered the Dominican Order and showed a taste for books and a talent for exact science. In 1765 he took charge of the great Bibliotheca Casanatensis at Santa Maria sopra Minerva. A Catholic Encyclopedia article presents a learned life of retirement and obscurity.

His four-volume catalogue of the Casanatense printed books, covering 1761 to 1788, stops unfinished at the letter L. He also catalogued Roman and Italian fifteenth-century editions, the latter reaching only the letter G at his death. He built a small observatory, observed the transits of Venus in 1761 and 1769, and tracked the great comet of 1769 across more than half the sky.

Giovanni Battista Giraldi, surnamed Cintio, was an Italian dramatist and novelist born at Ferrara in 1504, who died there in 1573. He studied philosophy and medicine at home, served briefly as secretary to the dukes of Ferrara, and then taught in turn at Mondovì, Turin, and Pavia. A Catholic Encyclopedia article ranks him among the leading literary critics of his time.

His criticism on writing epic, romance, and drama stands beside a pastoral play and an epic Ercole. He also wrote one comedy and nine tragedies, of which Orbecche is the best. He is remembered above all for the Ecatommiti, tales told by travelers fleeing the sack of Rome in 1527. Its seventh tale of the third decade gives the Moor of Venice later used in Shakespeare's Othello.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-fran:
Giovanni Francesco Grimaldi was an eclectic painter of the Bolognese school, born at Bologna in 1606, who died at Rome in 1680. A pupil of the Carracci, he made his mark after leaving Bologna for Rome, where Innocent X employed him on Vatican frescoes. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a landscape man who became a favorite of popes and kings.

Prince Pamfili had him decorate his villa with landscapes, then praised the work to Louis XIV, who brought Grimaldi to Paris through Mazarin. There he decorated two rooms of the Louvre and is said to have been knighted. Back in Rome he served Alexander VII and Clement IX, presided over the Academy of St. Luke, and etched landscapes with skill. His chief pictures hang in the Colonna palace and the Quirinal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-mari:
Giovanni Maria Cornoldi was a professor, author, and preacher born at Venice in 1822, who died at Rome in 1892. He entered the Jesuits in 1840, then taught philosophy for many years at Bressanone and Padua. From 1880 until his death he worked on the staff of Civiltà Cattolica at Rome and often preached at the Gesù. A Catholic Encyclopedia article presents an ardent disciple of St. Thomas.

His Lessons in Philosophy of 1872, translated into Latin as Philosophical Institutions after the mind of St. Thomas, explained Thomas's doctrine and answered Rosminianism. He also published a commentary on Dante's Divine Comedy, drawn from philosophy and theology. He founded academies in honor of St. Thomas at Bologna and Rome, and started two periodicals, La Scienza Italiana and the journal of the Academy of St. Thomas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giuseppe-verd:
Giuseppe Verdi was a composer born at Le Roncole near Parma in Italy on 10 October 1813, who died at Sant' Agata near Busseto on 27 January 1901. At ten he became organist of his village church, studied at Busseto under Provesi, then at Milan under Lavigna. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a career that ran from Oberto in 1839 to Falstaff in 1893.

Nabucco of 1842 and Ernani of 1844 made his fame. Rigoletto of 1851 opened a new phase, followed by Il Trovatore and La Traviata in 1853. Don Carlos of 1867 and Aida, produced at Cairo in 1871, mark a third style. Rumored to have laid down his pen after Aida, he astonished admirers with Otello in 1887 and, as an octogenarian, Falstaff in 1893.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guilio-carlo-:
Sinigaglia's mathematician Guilio Carlo De' Toschi Di, born in 1682, came late and alone to the subject that made him known. He shone at Rome's Collegio Clementino in everything except mathematics, which he disliked, yet after college he mastered it without a teacher, publishing his research in the Giornale de' Letterati d'Italia.

His best-known work measured and divided arcs of curves, above all the lemniscate, a figure-eight curve. He prized it so highly that he set the lemniscate with the words Deo veritatis gloria on his Produzioni Matematiche of 1750 and on his tomb. Mild in controversy and praised for clarity, he was also the father of twelve, one an archdeacon and one a Benedictine nun.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacopo-nardi:
Historian Jacopo Nardi was born at Florence in 1476 and died at Venice on 11 March 1563. His father Salvestro belonged to an old Florentine family from the city's suburbs. Jacopo followed Savonarola earnestly and witnessed his death. He backed the republican party and held various state offices. Yet he stayed friendly with the Medici after their return in 1512. He even composed pageants for them.

After taking part in the republican revolution of 1527, he was banished from Florence in 1530. He led exile efforts to return, pleading their cause against Duke Alessandro's tyranny before Charles V in 1536. He finally settled at Venice and died there in poverty. Contemporaries praised his upright and noble character. Before exile he wrote two comedies, L'Amicizia and I Due Felici Rivali. The entry presents a republican historian of principle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacopone-da-t:
Franciscan poet Jacopone da Todi was born at Todi in the early thirteenth century. He died at Collazzone about 1306. Very little about his life is certain. The oldest lives date only from the fifteenth century. A few earlier records exist, however.

The oldest authentic document bears his signature to a manifesto. Cardinals Jacopo and Pietro Colonna issued it against Boniface VIII on 10 May 1297. Angelo Clareno, writing about 1323, lists Jacobus Tudertus among spiritual friars. In 1294 those friars sent a deputation to Celestine V. They sought leave to live apart from the main Franciscan body. The entry weighs scant records against later legend. It presents a fiery poet-monk at odds with popes and order alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-baptist-:
John Baptist Albertrandi was a Polish Jesuit scholar called the Polish Polyhistor for the vastness of his learning. Born at Warsaw in 1731 of Italian extraction, he entered the Society of Jesus in 1748. He taught literature in Jesuit colleges for twelve years. He then took charge of the great Zaluski library, later seized by Russia as the nucleus of the imperial library.

As tutor to the primate's nephew he traveled Europe, copying manuscripts on Polish history by hand wherever he found them. What he could not copy he wrote out from memory, amassing over a hundred folio volumes in three years. Master of Greek, Latin, Hebrew, and most European tongues, he published a translation of Macquer's Roman History. He abridged Annals of Poland, wrote many Warsaw journal articles and a work on coins, and later became royal librarian and Bishop of Zenopolis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lodi:
Lodi is a diocese and trading city in Lombardy, on the right bank of the Adda, dealing in silk, wool, majolica, and cement work. Its Lombard cathedral, raised in 1158, holds Campi paintings, a crypt, and a rich treasury of codices and a great silver monstrance.

Old Lodi, Laus Pompeia, clashed often with Milan, which razed it in 1025, 1111, and 1158. Barbarossa built the new city in 1160, and it stayed loyal to him, later joining the Lombard League against his son. Lodi also sealed a peace of Milan, Venice, and Florence in 1454, and saw Napoleon seize its bridge in 1796.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lorenzo-di-cr:
Lorenzo di Credi was a Florentine painter, born in 1459 and dead in 1537, whose name came from his first master, the goldsmith Credi. He then trained under Verrocchio beside Perugino and Leonardo da Vinci, and clung to Leonardo's manner with great success.

A devout follower of Savonarola, he painted portraits and church pictures prized across Florence and beyond, from Pistoia to Berlin, London, and Turin. His colour glows and his design charms, yet his drapery stays stiff as metal, a trace of goldsmith training. Slow and painstaking, he ground his own colours and finished each work with fine care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marcantonio-r:
Marcantonio Raimondi was an engraver born at Bologna in 1475, or 1480, and dead there in 1530, or 1534. He trained under the goldsmith and niellist Francia, often signing M-A. F. for his master. His earliest plate, Pyramus and Thisbe of 1505, still shows goldsmith shading.

Seeing Durer's plates, he copied them in 1506 so well they sold as originals, until Venice, on Durer's complaint, made him add his own initials. Mars and Cupid of 1508 shows him master of technique. In Rome he engraved Michelangelo's lost Climbers cartoon, drawing Raphael's praise as the finest print he had seen. Raphael gave him outline drawings to elaborate, and their friendship made Raimondi's fame match Raphael's. Later, obscene plates for Romano and Aretino landed him in Clement's prison, freed at Cardinal de Medici's plea. He fled the sack of Rome in 1527, leaving fortune and plates behind, and left about six hundred plates in all.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-ricc:
Nicholas Riccardi, a Dominican theologian and preacher born at Genoa in 1585, is the subject of this Catholic Encyclopedia entry. After study in Spain, he joined the Dominicans, taught Thomistic theology at Pincia, and moved to Rome in 1621, where Pope Urban VIII trusted him with high office.

Called "The Marvel" by Philip III of Spain for his preaching, Riccardi became Master of the Sacred Palace in 1629 and papal preacher soon after. Twenty surviving works are listed, with sermons for Advent and Lent, commentaries on every book of Scripture, and a 1627 history of the Council of Trent among them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-odorico-rayna:
Oratorian historian Odorico Raynaldi, born at Treviso in 1595, carried Baronius's church annals from 1198 to 1565. Of patrician birth and schooled at Parma and Padua, he joined the Rome Oratorians, won twice election as superior general, and turned down Innocent X's offer of the Vatican Library.

Published at Rome from 1646 to 1677, his continuation reproduces many original documents, making it prized despite slips in dates and criticism. Raynaldi also issued Latin and Italian excerpts from Baronius and his own work, and died at Rome in 1671. He published excerpts in Latin and Italian from Baronius and from his own continuation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pellegrino-ti:
Pellegrino Tibaldi was a Bolognese painter, decorator, and architect of the later sixteenth century. Born at Bologna in 1527, he studied under Bagnacavallo and steeped himself in Michelangelo's work. His early commissions came largely from Cardinal Poggi, for palaces and chapels at Bologna, Loreto, and Rome. This short Catholic Encyclopedia life follows a career split between Italy and Spain.

In 1586 Philip II called him to Spain, where he painted the lower cloisters of the Escorial after wiping away his predecessors' work. His finest achievement there was the decoration of the Escorial library. After nine years in Spain he returned to Italy, settled at Milan, and became architect of its cathedral. He died at Milan about 1592, and his works survive at Bologna and Dresden.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-periodi: Periodi was the name under which three early witnesses quote the writings now known as the Pseudo-Clementines: Epiphanius, Jerome, and the anthology called the Philocalia. This brief Catholic Encyclopedia entry records that usage and nothing more. It is a cross-reference stub, sending readers on to the article on the Clementines for the works themselves and their history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-gassen:
Pierre Gassendi was a French philosopher and scientist, born at Champtercier near Digne on 22 January 1592. He studied Latin and rhetoric at Digne and philosophy at Aix. He succeeded his rhetoric teacher at sixteen and his philosophy teacher at nineteen. Aided by patrons Gautier and Peiresc, he entered the church and mastered Greek and Hebrew at Aix.

In 1645, on Richelieu's recommendation, the king named him professor of mathematics at the Collège Royal, where his lectures ran astronomical rather than mathematical and produced the Institutio Astronomica two years later. An amateur astronomer with a notebook kept from 1618 to 1652, he observed Mercury's 1631 transit, predicted by Kepler, by projecting the sun's image on paper. He wrote to Galileo, Kepler, and Cassini, and held that the earth moves round the sun, though unproved. Retiring and unpretentious, he never missed Mass on Sundays and feasts and died at Paris in 1655.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sant-angelo-d:
Sant'Angelo de' Lombardi, a diocese in Avellino province in southern Italy, grew from a city founded by the Lombards at an unknown date, near sulphurous springs. Almost wholly destroyed in 1664, it became a bishopric under Gregory VII, though its first known bishop is Thomas in 1179, when it answered to Conza. Its short entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia packs three sees into one.

In 1540, under Bishop Rinaldo de' Cancellieri, it joined Bisaccia, ancient Romulea, a Samnite town taken by Rome in 295 before Christ and a bishopric by 1179. In 1818 Monteverde joined as well, its earliest known bishop Mario dating from 1049. The united see holds nine parishes with 40,000 souls, forty-five secular priests, some religious, three monastic houses, and a girls' school, with the learned Dominican Ignazio Cianti among its bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-todi:
Todi is a diocese in central Italy, directly subject to the Holy See, set on a steep hill above the Tiber valley. Its triple walls still stand: an inner Umbrian or Etruscan wall of rough travertine, a Roman middle wall, and an outer wall of the sixth or seventh century. The Lombard-style cathedral holds ten pillars of eastern marble, and Santa Maria della Consolazione, begun in 1508, counts among the finest works of the Renaissance.

Called Tutere on pre-Roman coins and Tuder by the Romans, the town was sacked by Crassus in 83 BC. Augustus made it a colony, and it held out against Totila in the Gothic wars. In the eleventh century it became a republic, drew up statutes under the jurist Bartolo in 1340, and stayed almost always Ghibelline in long conflict with Perugia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ubaldo-girald:
Ubaldo Giraldi, known in religion as Ubaldus of St Cajetan, was an Italian canonist born in 1692. He died in 1775. A member of the Piarist order, he served twice as assistant general-councillor of his congregation. He governed its Roman province, headed the Piarist college at Rome, and acted as apostolic examiner for the Roman clergy. His working life joined teaching, administration, and the study of church law in eighteenth-century Rome.

His books show a compiler's mind rather than a theorist's. He issued an enlarged edition of Maschat's Institutes of Canon Law. Then he gathered the chief texts of the Decretals and the Council of Trent, with the papal rulings that explain or change them. He added only a short commentary of his own. His lasting reputation rests on a new annotated edition of Barbosa's great work on parish priests, a tool for working clergy rather than a treatise.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ulissi-aldrov:
Ulisse Aldrovandi was an Italian naturalist born at Bologna on 11 September 1522. He died there on 10 November 1607, though some sources give 1605. Educated at Bologna and Padua, he took his medical doctorate in 1553 and became professor of natural history at Bologna. At his urging the city's senate founded a botanical garden in 1568, with Aldrovandi as its first director. He also served as inspector of pharmacies, a post that set him quarrelling with apothecaries and physicians until Pope Gregory XIII upheld him in 1576.

Travel, spending, and collecting filled his life. His herbaria and cabinets in botany and zoology became, by his bequest, the nucleus of the Bologna Museum. His herbarium counts as the first collection worthy of the name. His printed works, vast and richly illustrated, spread his observations across Europe. The entry presents a Renaissance collector whose fortune went into specimens and books, laying groundwork for natural history as a public science.

doe-osti-3374218-initial-testing-of-prom: Promess presses got shielding-initially-tested, and this DOE text covers the testing. The pages detail the findings. The engineers get their data. The shielding was press. The data were engineer. The Promess were initial. The testing were initial. The engineers were data.
erewhon-revisited-twenty-years-later-bot:
Samuel Butler returned to his upside-down country in Erewhon Revisited, published in 1901, twenty years after the original discoverer's escape. His preface asks what followed when Higgs ascended in a balloon with Arowhena before the Erewhonians' eyes: a miracle demanding a religion. The answer fills the sequel, told partly by Higgs's son.

The younger Higgs travels into Erewhon and finds his father worshipped as the Sunchild, with professors Hanky and Panky guarding the new faith's evidence and quarreling over nuggets in a hollow tree. Butler aims at the founding of Christianity by parody, and at his own earlier book. The satire is gentler and sadder than Erewhon, and its target, respectable belief, has lost none of its polish.
first-across-the-continent-the-story-of-:
Noah Brooks retold the Lewis and Clark expedition in First Across the Continent, covering the exploring years 1804 to 1806. His first chapter, A Great Transaction in Land, begins with America's astonishment at Napoleon's sale of Louisiana for fifteen million dollars, arranged by Livingston and Monroe with Barbe-Marbois. Jefferson's explorers then set out to learn what the nation had bought.

Brooks follows the journals closely: rivers, hailstorms that drop rain and snow within miles of each other, capsized canoes, and merchandise dried slowly after soakings. Sacagawea, the Mandan winter, and the Pacific arrival all appear in journal language. Written for general readers, the book keeps the expedition's daily texture while making its national meaning plain.
govdocs-archive_org-meditations-on-the-p:
Julius Evola climbed mountains as a young man, and in Meditations on the Peaks he treats the high ranges as more than sport. For Evola the mountain is a symbol of spiritual ascent, and climbing becomes a discipline of the inner life.

The essays set out his doctrine of the mountain: height as purity, effort as initiation, the summit as a meeting with the sacred. He writes against turning mountaineering into tourism or athletics alone. The book gathers his mountain writings into one of his most personal works, where landscape and metaphysics are treated as the same subject.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig: Cheddi Jagan, the elected leader of British Guiana, was driven from office in 1964 after a campaign of pressure in which the CIA played a covert part. This briefing-book page presents the record of those operations in the small South American colony. The evidence here is the title alone, so the specific documents cannot be named. The case matters beyond its size: it showed Washington applying Cold War covert methods in the Caribbean basin, against a leftist who had won at the ballot box.
heidi:
Johanna Spyri wrote Heidi, the story of a Swiss orphan girl sent to live with her grandfather, Alm-Uncle, in a hut above an Alpine village. Heidi thrives among goats, hay beds, and mountain air, visiting the blind grandmother of goatherd Peter. Then a housekeeper's plan takes her to Frankfurt as companion to Clara Sesemann, a girl who cannot walk.

In the great house Heidi sickens with homesickness and walks in her sleep, taken for a ghost. Sent home, she recovers, learns to read, and softens her grandfather's hard heart. Clara's later visit to the mountain brings the famous ending. Spyri wrote for children and for those who love children, as her title page said.
john-thorndyke-s-cases-related-by-christ:
John Thorndyke's Cases is a set of detective stories by R. Austin Freeman, told by Christopher Jervis. Thorndyke is a doctor-detective whose cases turn on exact physical evidence. Eight cases fill the book, from The Man with the Nailed Shoes to A Message from the Deep Sea. Photographs and drawings of clues appear throughout the volume.

The cases include a stranger's latchkey, a blue sequin, a Moabite cipher, and a mandarin's pearl. An aluminium dagger and an anthropologist at large round out the set. The picture list shows hair sections, sand from a pillow, and a sergeant's sketch. Freeman built these tales on careful forensic method, clue by clue.
nasa-tm-19640019268-the-electrical-chara: Goddard Space Flight Center issued this study on March 30, 1964. It treats the electrical traits of silicon solar cells that have been exposed to radiation. How those traits shift with temperature is the report's stated focus. Solar cells power most satellites, and space radiation slowly harms them. The hosted sample preserves only the report's title page, with no readable abstract or body text, so its data cannot be described from the sample itself.
nasa-tm-19660020186-extraterrestrial-app:
H K Herglotz presented this study at a Marshall space science seminar in February 1966, issued on April 20, 1966. X-ray diffraction can name the elements in a sample and identify many compounds and minerals. Herglotz calls it a promising candidate for exploring the surfaces of the Moon and of Earth-like planets. That promise holds only if gear fit for space can be built, he adds.

He describes the method's fundamentals first. Then he turns to the difficulties of using it off Earth. Weight, power, and handling samples without human hands all stand in the way. Later lunar and Mars landers did carry such instruments, along the path this paper surveyed.
nasa-tm-19670022936-flight-test-of-a-31-:
John S. Preisser, Clinton V. Eckstrom, and Harold N. Murrow, of NASA's Langley Research Center in Virginia, flight-tested a parachute in this report. The canopy was a modified ringsail, about thirty-one feet across. It deployed above the speed of sound, under the NASA Planetary Entry Parachute Program.

A mortar fired the parachute out behind an instrumented payload at Mach 1.39. The canopy reached line stretch in a fraction of a second, then inflated quickly to full open. The peak opening load came just as the canopy filled. The test proved a big ringsail could open safely at supersonic speed and very low air pressure.
nasa-tm-19680013268-viewing-devices-for-:
Lawrence A. Mueller and David W. Medwid of NASA's Lewis Research Center wrote this 1968 memorandum on windows for hot mercury systems. Space power units that boil and condense liquid metals need a clear way to watch the flow inside. The authors studied windows for a mercury condensing tube and a mercury boiler outlet tube.

Matching how the window, sealants, and support expand with heat proved central to the design. The condensing tube window was tested with flowing mercury at high heat and pressure, then shaken at room temperature. The boiler window was heated in a furnace under gas pressure. Sealants, window shapes, and metal to glass joints were all checked under harsh test conditions.
nasa-tm-19680028473-melting-relationship:
A. F. Koster van Groos, a resident research associate at Goddard Space Flight Center, and P. J. Wyllie, of the University of Chicago, studied melting in a rock-like chemical system under pressure. Their mixture joins a sodium aluminum silicon oxide with salt and water, squeezed at one kilobar. Such systems help geologists read how real magmas melt and crystallize deep underground.

Chapters describe the starting materials, the pressure apparatus, and how each mineral phase was identified. Results follow for the dry salt mixture and for the mixture with water added. A long discussion traces courses of crystallization and the effect of pressure itself. The report closes with petrological applications, tying the laboratory melts to natural rocks.
nasa-tm-19690029214-experimental-investi:
James E. Calogeras of Lewis Research Center investigated dynamic distortion in a supersonic inlet in this October 1969 memorandum. Tests ran in the Lewis 10-by-10-Foot Supersonic Wind Tunnel at Mach 2.50. The inlet had sixty percent internal contraction and fed a J85-GE-13 turbojet engine.

Average pressure fluctuations of only a small share of total pressure could completely degrade stall margin at certain engine speeds, he found. Vortex generators suppressed dynamic distortion at off-design conditions much better than throat bleed did. The engine's presence changed neither the size nor the spread of the distortion. Inlet-engine compatibility work like this protects engines from sudden stalls in supersonic flight.
nasa-tm-19700009496-flight-control-of-th:
M. P. Frank of the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston wrote this paper in December 1969. He had presented it in Tokyo in August that year. It explains how flight controllers in Houston ran the Apollo lunar landing mission.

Frank first describes the worldwide tracking and data network that fed the control center. He then covers the center itself and how it passed spacecraft and crew data to the flight control team. The paper lays out how the control team was organized and which skills it drew on. It ends with a detailed account of the flight control work during a landing mission.
nasa-tm-19710008389-motor-starting-chara:
David S. Repas and Robert J. Frye of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in March 1971. It records how a modified Lundell alternator behaves when it starts as a motor. The machine was designed for a single-shaft Brayton-cycle space power system.

To start the whole power loop, the alternator itself must spin up first. The team started it as an induction motor and measured the run. They logged armature current, shaft speed, and field voltage through the start. Torque was then figured from the measured speeding-up and the rotor's inertia. A power system that cannot start itself is dead weight in orbit.
notes-and-queries-index-of-volume-2-may-:
Volume two of Notes and Queries ran from May to December 1850, and this file holds its index. The journal served literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists, per its title page. Its motto stayed Captain Cuttle's rule: when found, make a note of. Entries point by page to notes, queries, and replies.

Under A, a note treats the solemnization of matrimony, and many pages treat aerostation, or balloon flight. The Agapemone, Agincourt, and a cure for ague by spiders all appear. Ale draper gets a meaning hunt, and Alfred's Orosius a note. Apricot and peach etymology closes the sampled run. No topic was too small for its pages.
on-the-method-of-zadig-essay-1-from-scie:
Thomas Henry Huxley wrote this essay on scientific method. It is essay one from Science and Hebrew Tradition. His subtitle calls it retrospective prophecy in science. Zadig is a figure from a tale by Voltaire. Cuvier had praised Zadig's sure marks of reasoning.

Zadig retired to the banks of the Euphrates River. Patient study of plants and animals sharpened his sight. He learned to spot minute differences in similar things. Huxley uses him to show how science reasons backward. Small clues reveal past events, as tracks reveal animals. He lived, the tale says, at Babylon under King Moabdar. No king list since found names that king at all.
podcast-dannyjones-5_vzzUlAoDI:
Fraudster Matthew Cox returns for KONCRETE number 46 with Danny Jones. Fans keep asking for Cox back on the show. This visit is billed as a look inside a pathological liar's mind.

Cox has served time for huge mortgage fraud schemes. He now tells his story as both warning and show. Jones asks how lying became habit, craft, and income. Cox brings props and treats the talk like a stage act. The episode lets a proud con man explain his own thinking, which makes it both gripping and hard to fully trust.
podcast-joerogan-8xRz8ra9mdI:
Duncan Trussell's episode 1530 of the Joe Rogan Experience finds the comedian in his familiar role: half jester, half seeker. Trussell had by then become one of the show's defining guests, known for turning any topic into a trip through myth and mind.

The conversation floats across psychedelics, the self, and the strange comfort of not knowing. Rogan grounds the riffs with stories from his own life and work. Longtime listeners will hear the pair's rhythm at its smoothest here, while new listeners get a fair sample of why Trussell's visits are treated as events by the show's fans.
report-of-mr-w-e-cormack-s-journey-in-se:
W. E. Cormack read this report of his journey in search of the Red Indians of Newfoundland before the Boeothick Institution at St. John's. The meeting was held on January 12, 1828, with A. W. Desbarres in the chair. The Institution had been formed to open contact with the Red Indians and to record their history.

Cormack, the Institution's president, outlines his expedition rather than giving its full detail. His party held three men besides himself: an able Abenakie man from Canada, an elder Mountaineer from Labrador, and a young Micmack native of the island. They had meant to start at White Bay and travel south, but weather blocked the plan.
targum-or-metrical-translations-from-thi:
George Borrow made Targum, a set of verse renderings drawn from thirty tongues and dialects, picked from a vast heap of work built up over years of language study. Borrow offers the pieces with frank doubt about his own success in spots.

He argues that the hardest part of verse rendering is not the words but the cast and turn of the source. He praises Fairfax, who put Tasso's Jerusalem into English octave rhyme, as a rare master of that art. Borrow also holds that a nation's tone shows best in its songs, from soft Persian airs to bold Danish war ditties. Readers get a wide, odd tour of world song.
the-kasi-dah-of-ha-ji-abdu-el-yezdi:
The Kasîdah of Hâjî Abdû El-Yezdî calls itself a lay of the higher law. The author's friend and pupil F. B. translated and annotated it. A note to the reader is signed from Vienna. November 1880 is its date. The note lays out the poem's principles. Happiness and misery are equally divided in the world. Self-cultivation, with due regard to others, is life's sole object. The affections and the gift of pity are man's highest joys. Judgment should be suspended, the note adds. Facts deserve proper suspicion.

The poem opens at nightfall. The waning moon walks forth to rule the later night. A star's sparkle crowns it. F. B. concedes the work looks destructive. It is essentially reconstructive, he says. Curious readers are sent to the volume's end for details. Richard Burton's poem wears a Persian mask here. It asks to be read as wisdom, not narrative.
the-method-by-which-the-causes-of-the-pr:
Thomas H. Huxley's lecture on the method for discovering the causes of the present and past condition of organic nature was delivered to working men at the Museum of Practical Geology in 1863. It forms the third of six lectures on Darwin's Origin of Species. Huxley recaps two earlier lectures on the extent of the subject. He then turns to the great problem: what knowledge we have of the causes behind organic phenomena.

An objection meets him at the threshold, from worthy people who hold that vital phenomena lie outside ordinary inquiry. Such objectors call the origin of life miraculous and further questions presumptuous. Huxley answers with the story of Diogenes, who refuted a sophist's proof that motion was impossible by simply getting up and walking. Science, he says, replies the same way, by pointing to the immense mass of facts already systematized under morphology, development, and distribution.
the-religion-of-the-samurai-a-study-of-z: Kaiten Nukariya taught at colleges in Tokyo. He studies Zen philosophy and discipline here. China and Japan both fall within his scope. The work is dated 1913. Contents promise a full introduction first. It covers Buddhist schools and the Mahayana view of life. It covers Zen's denial of scriptural authority. Its iconoclastic attitude gets a section too. Physical and mental training close the survey. A history of Zen in China follows, starting with Bodhidharma. Only the title pages and contents list are present here.
